 View Comments Bruce Meyer, interim executive director of the Major League Baseball Players Association, speaks on the field before Game 1 of the World Series in Milwaukee. Kayla Wolf/AP Photo/Kayla Wolf MILWAUKEE — Forget market sizes and payrolls for a minute, if that’s possible, and appreciate this World Series for the two teams on the field, not what they represent as baseball races toward another labor war. 
 The Brewers were the best team in the National League and the Rays the best in the American League. They’re not proxies in the fight over whether baseball should have a salary cap. 
 But that can’t be avoided. For the MLB Players Association, this World Series proves the game is thriving, and a cap isn’t needed to give teams in smaller cities hope. 
 For commissioner Rob Manfred and the owners he represents, it’s the other side of the coin. 
 “It’s good for baseball to have two small markets like this,” Manfred said. “It shows that we leave a lot on the table in some of our smaller markets by not having them have an opportunity to compete on a regular basis.”

 Players Association chief Bruce Meyer doesn’t believe that’s necessary. 
 “None of this has to be happening,” Meyer said. “The owners made a choice. They’re going to make a choice, presumably to lock the players out. They’re not required to do that. They’re apparently going to once again.” 
 Related : Cam Booser’s wild ride from construction to the majors now includes World Series trip with the Rays Meyer is the interim head of the union, taking the job in February after Tony Clark resigned amidst a scandal. He’s tasked with finding a way to make a deal without accepting a salary cap, something the Players Association has resisted for decades. 
 Manfred, who plans to retire after the 2028 season, hopes to create a system that narrows the gap between the sport’s financial behemoths and smaller-market teams without baseball missing games in 2027. 
 In his mind, the Brewers are an example of what is wrong, not what is right. 
 “I think the small markets operate at a disadvantage economically,” Manfred said. “They just don’t have the resources that our bigger markets do. 
 “I mean, [this World Series] is the best evidence. Look, the Brewers have been a well-run franchise forever. It’s been 40 years since [they’re] here. Once every 40 years is not enough. 
 “If you look at the data, our larger markets have a very statistically significant advantage in terms of making the playoffs and going deeper in the playoffs.” 
 Meyer sees that as an excuse to pay players less and put more money in the pockets of the owners. 
 “I think the fact that they’re doubling down on the cap now, in the wake of what’s happening with this World Series just illustrates that it’s not about competitive balance,” he said. 
 “It’s not about teams not having hope. It’s about their desire — which they’ve had for decades — to have a system that artificially suppresses player salaries, player freedom of movement, removes player guarantees, and limits flexibility in all different areas, guts the amateur entry system. 
 “You know, the rest of it is a charade.” 
 Related : Brewers are living their “Glory Days” after beating Rays in World Series opener Baseball’s last attempt to institute a salary cap, in 1994, led to a long strike and the cancellation of the World Series. Both the ’94 and ’95 seasons were shortened. 
 At a time when the game is enjoying increased attendance, higher television ratings, and an uptick in cultural cachet, a work stoppage would be ruinous. 
 The popularity of the World Baseball Classic and baseball’s return to the Olympics in 2028 suggest there’s even more room for growth. 
 The success of the Brewers and Rays aside, the payroll gap between the Dodgers, Mets, and Yankees, and the Marlins, Rockies, and Nationals is too large. The question is whether that can be bridged without the owners insisting on a cap. 
 To hear Manfred and Meyer talk at the World Series, the sides are miles apart. But that was also true during the contentious negotiations after the 2021 season, and the ’22 season was pushed back by only a week. 
 “Re-thinking where you are is a really important part of trying to make a deal, and it’s actually a skill in collective bargaining,” Manfred said. 
 Meyer hasn’t seen any evidence of that. 
 “In negotiations, they’ve made clear that at this point they’re not willing to talk about anything outside of their cap system,” he said. 
 It’s going to be a torturous offseason. Enjoy the games while you can.
